claims.claim_text: In March 2021, a fire destroyed OVHcloud's SBG2 datacenter in Strasbourg, France.
claims.rationale: The incident is real, but the primary OVHcloud incident page is outside the current allowlist.

claims.claim_text: Thousands of OVHcloud customers lost data permanently.
claims.anchor_text: Thousands of customers lost data permanently.
claims.suggested_rewrite: Customers without off-site backups can turn a facility loss into permanent data loss.
claims.rationale: The precise customer-loss scale is not backed by an allowlisted primary source and should be generalized.

claims.claim_text: An unnamed e-commerce company lost an entire Kubernetes cluster in the OVH fire, took 11 days to recover, and lost more than 2 million euros.
claims.anchor_text: One e-commerce company running Kubernetes on bare metal in that single facility lost their entire cluster -- etcd data, persistent volumes, application state, everything. They had backups, but the backups were stored on the same physical infrastructure. Recovery took 11 days. Revenue loss exceeded 2 million euros.
claims.suggested_rewrite: A Kubernetes cluster whose backups live in the same physical failure domain can lose both primary state and recovery copies in the same disaster, turning a restore into a rebuild.
claims.rationale: This is a fake-precise war story with no attributable source.

claims.claim_text: An unnamed logistics company in the same datacenter had zero data loss, four minutes of downtime, 15-minute etcd snapshot replication, and 90-second DNS failover.
claims.anchor_text: Six months later, a logistics company in the same datacenter came through the same fire with zero data loss and four minutes of downtime. They ran an active-passive Kubernetes setup across two sites, with Velero backing up to S3-compatible storage in a different facility, etcd snapshots replicated every 15 minutes, and DNS-based failover that redirected traffic within 90 seconds.
claims.suggested_rewrite: A contrasting DR design keeps backup storage and replicated cluster state in a separate facility, maintains a standby site, and rehearses DNS failover so recovery follows tested operational steps instead of improvisation.
claims.rationale: This named-incident-adjacent anecdote has exact timings and technical details but no attributable source.

claims.claim_text: Stretched etcd clusters have a hard 10 ms RTT latency limit.
claims.anchor_text: - Why stretched etcd clusters have a hard 10ms RTT latency limit
claims.suggested_rewrite: - Why stretched etcd clusters require low, measured RTT and careful etcd latency testing
claims.rationale: The exact universal 10 ms limit is too strong for generic Kubernetes and should be replaced with latency-tested guidance.

claims.claim_text: Active-active Kubernetes requires less than 10 ms RTT between sites.
claims.anchor_text: | **Network requirement** | <10ms RTT between sites | Any bandwidth |
claims.suggested_rewrite: | **Network requirement** | Very low, validated RTT and jitter between sites | Enough bandwidth for backup and replication windows |
claims.rationale: The exact RTT threshold is an unsupported rule of thumb.

claims.claim_text: Active-active costs 2x infrastructure and active-passive costs 1.3-1.5x.
claims.anchor_text: | **Cost** | 2x infrastructure | 1.3-1.5x (standby can be smaller) |
claims.suggested_rewrite: | **Cost** | Roughly duplicated infrastructure | Lower than full duplication when the standby site is smaller |
claims.rationale: The cost multipliers are illustrative, while the general DR tradeoff between cost, complexity, and recovery posture is well documented.

claims.claim_text: Active-active requires RPO=0, RTO<60s, sites within 10 ms RTT, and 2x infrastructure.
claims.anchor_text: **Active-active** requires: RPO=0, RTO<60s, sites within 10ms RTT, budget for 2x infra.
claims.suggested_rewrite: **Active-active** is appropriate when the workload truly needs near-zero data loss and very fast recovery, the sites have measured low-latency connectivity, and the budget can support duplicated capacity.
claims.rationale: The exact RTO, RTT, and cost thresholds are presented as universal requirements without a primary source.

claims.claim_text: Active-passive works when RPO of 15-60 minutes is acceptable.
claims.anchor_text: **Active-passive** works when: RPO of 15-60 min is acceptable, sites are distant, budget is constrained.
claims.suggested_rewrite: **Active-passive** works when some backup lag is acceptable, sites are distant, and budget or operational complexity makes full active-active impractical.
claims.rationale: The specific RPO range is illustrative guidance, not a sourced technical threshold.

claims.claim_text: The RTT table gives exact etcd behavior bands starting with less than 2 ms as excellent.
claims.anchor_text: | <2ms | Excellent | Same rack / same building |
claims.suggested_rewrite: | Very low and stable | Best case | Same rack / same building |
claims.rationale: The precise latency band is unsupported and should be expressed qualitatively.

claims.claim_text: The RTT table says 2-5 ms is good for same campus or metro stretched etcd.
claims.anchor_text: | 2-5ms | Good, slight latency increase | Same campus / metro |
claims.suggested_rewrite: | Low and stable | Usually workable after testing | Same campus / metro |
claims.rationale: The exact latency band is unsupported and should be framed as a tested condition.

claims.claim_text: The RTT table says 5-10 ms is acceptable with tuning.
claims.anchor_text: | 5-10ms | Acceptable with tuning | Same metro, dedicated fiber |
claims.suggested_rewrite: | Low but jitter-sensitive | Requires load testing and tuning | Same metro, dedicated fiber |
claims.rationale: The exact latency band is unsupported and should be replaced with measured guidance.

claims.claim_text: The RTT table says 10-20 ms causes degraded etcd behavior and leader-election risk.
claims.anchor_text: | 10-20ms | Degraded, leader election risk | Not recommended |
claims.suggested_rewrite: | Noticeable WAN latency | High risk under load | Avoid stretched etcd unless supported by product guidance |
claims.rationale: The exact threshold is unsupported as a generic Kubernetes rule.

claims.claim_text: The RTT table says greater than 20 ms is unstable and creates split-brain risk.
claims.anchor_text: | >20ms | Unstable, split brain risk | Do not stretch etcd |
claims.suggested_rewrite: | High WAN latency | Not suitable for stretched etcd | Use separate clusters and asynchronous DR |
claims.rationale: The precise threshold and split-brain wording are unsupported in this generic form.

claims.claim_text: For 5-10 ms RTT, tune etcd to compensate.
claims.span_hint: line 106 | Stretched Clusters and the etcd Latency Wall
claims.anchor_text: For 5-10ms RTT, tune etcd to compensate:
claims.suggested_rewrite: When RTT and jitter are no longer local-network low, test etcd under load and tune only with a measured latency budget:
claims.rationale: The exact RTT band is an unsupported tuning trigger.

claims.claim_text: RTO and RPO are disaster-recovery objectives: RTO measures recovery time, and RPO measures acceptable data-loss window.
claims.rationale: The AWS Well-Architected DR objectives page directly defines RTO and RPO.

claims.claim_text: Velero can use S3-compatible object storage such as MinIO as a backup target.
claims.span_hint: line 160 | Velero with MinIO for Backup
claims.rationale: Velero's MinIO documentation shows S3-compatible configuration using the AWS provider, s3Url, and path-style access.

claims.claim_text: Velero's --use-node-agent and --default-volumes-to-fs-backup flags enable file-system-level volume backup behavior.
claims.span_hint: line 160 | Velero with MinIO for Backup
claims.rationale: Velero's file-system backup documentation directly describes node-agent setup and the default-volumes-to-fs-backup behavior.

claims.claim_text: Velero backs up Kubernetes API resources and supports targeted restore of resources such as namespaces.
claims.span_hint: lines 156 and 198 | Velero and etcd backup comparison
claims.rationale: The Velero architecture documentation describes backing up and restoring Kubernetes resources through the API.

claims.claim_text: etcd is Kubernetes' backing store for all cluster data, and Kubernetes documentation covers etcd snapshot backup and restore.
claims.span_hint: line 198 | etcd Snapshot Backup and Restore
claims.rationale: The Kubernetes etcd administration page directly states etcd stores all cluster data and documents snapshot save and restore.

claims.claim_text: The etcd snapshot status command reports hash, revision, key count, and size.
claims.rationale: The Kubernetes etcd snapshot examples show snapshot status output with hash, revision, total keys, and total size.

claims.claim_text: DNS TTL is only a suggestion, and operators should budget 2-5 minutes of stale DNS even with a 30-second TTL.
claims.anchor_text: > **Warning**: DNS TTL is a suggestion, not a command. Budget for 2-5 minutes of stale DNS in your RTO, even with a 30-second TTL.
claims.suggested_rewrite: > **Warning**: DNS TTL controls cache lifetime, but failover still depends on recursive resolvers, local caches, and client retry behavior. Budget extra propagation and retry time in your RTO even when the authoritative record has a low TTL.
claims.rationale: The exact stale-DNS interval is unsupported, and the TTL wording overstates the protocol behavior.

claims.claim_text: etcd stores every key twice, a 5 MB snapshot contains about 2.5 MB of unique data, and cluster state exists in three places simultaneously.
claims.anchor_text: 1. **etcd stores everything twice.** Every key lives in both a B-tree index and BoltDB. A 5MB snapshot contains ~2.5MB of unique data. The API server also caches resources in memory, so the cluster state exists in three places simultaneously.
claims.suggested_rewrite: 1. **Kubernetes control-plane state has layers.** etcd provides durable storage for cluster state, while API servers and controllers may keep caches in memory, so recovery planning needs to account for both durable state and control-plane behavior after restart.
claims.rationale: The storage-ratio and duplication claims are unsourced and too precise.

claims.claim_text: The largest known stretched Kubernetes cluster spans two datacenters 40 km apart with 0.8 ms RTT, runs over 2,000 nodes, took six months to tune, and most similar attempts fail within a year.
claims.anchor_text: 2. **The largest known stretched Kubernetes cluster** spans two datacenters 40km apart on dark fiber with 0.8ms RTT, running over 2,000 nodes. The team spent six months tuning before production. Most organizations that attempt this scale fail within the first year.
claims.suggested_rewrite: 2. **Stretched Kubernetes clusters are rare and operationally demanding.** Treat them as a specialized design that requires measured latency, failure-domain analysis, and repeated failover testing before production.
claims.rationale: This is an unattributed war story with exact scale, distance, latency, duration, and failure-rate claims.

claims.claim_text: Heptio Ark became Velero as of the v0.11.0 rename.
claims.rationale: The Velero migration documentation directly states that Heptio Ark was renamed Velero.

claims.claim_text: VMware completed its acquisition of Heptio in 2018, and Heptio was led by Joe Beda and Craig McLuckie.
claims.rationale: VMware's acquisition announcement directly confirms the acquisition and leadership names.

claims.claim_text: Joe Beda and Craig McLuckie were among the original creators of Kubernetes.
claims.rationale: The Kubernetes anniversary post discusses the original creation of Kubernetes and names Joe Beda and Craig McLuckie in that origin story.

claims.claim_text: A 500-node cluster's etcd snapshot is typically 50-150 MB and often restores in under 30 seconds.
claims.anchor_text: 4. **A 500-node cluster's etcd snapshot** is typically 50-150MB yet contains every Kubernetes resource. This compact size makes etcd snapshots the fastest restore path, often completing in under 30 seconds.
claims.suggested_rewrite: 4. **etcd snapshots can be a compact full-cluster recovery artifact.** Their size and restore time depend on object count, history, compaction, storage speed, and control-plane conditions, so measure them in your own cluster.
claims.rationale: The snapshot size and restore-duration numbers are unsupported benchmarks.

claims.claim_text: DNS TTL defaults are 300-3600 seconds, and failover records should be 30-60 seconds.
claims.anchor_text: | DNS TTL too high | Defaults are 300-3600s | Set 30-60s for failover records |
claims.suggested_rewrite: | DNS TTL too high | Long cache lifetimes delay failover | Set low TTLs for failover records and test resolver behavior |
claims.rationale: DNS default TTLs vary by provider and zone, so the numeric range should not be universalized.

claims.claim_text: If RTT is greater than 10 ms, use active-passive instead of stretching etcd.
claims.anchor_text: | Stretching etcd over high latency | Wanting active-active | Use active-passive if RTT >10ms |
claims.suggested_rewrite: | Stretching etcd over high latency | Wanting active-active | Use active-passive when measured latency and jitter make etcd quorum unsafe |
claims.rationale: The exact RTT cutoff repeats the unsupported universal threshold.

claims.claim_text: Velero defaults to resource-only backups.
claims.anchor_text: | Ignoring PV data in backups | Velero defaults to resource-only | Enable `--default-volumes-to-fs-backup` |
claims.suggested_rewrite: | Ignoring PV data in backups | Volume backup behavior depends on snapshot and file-system backup configuration | Enable and test the right volume backup path for your storage class |
claims.rationale: Velero backup behavior depends on volume snapshots, file-system backup settings, and provider support, so the row is oversimplified.
